extra.message: User input from request.json['search'] is concatenated directly into a SQL query string using Python % string formatting, then executed via db.engine.execute(). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data from the database.

request.url (user-controlled) is interpolated into an HTML template string via %s formatting and then passed to render_template_string(). Jinja2 will evaluate any template syntax in the URL (e.g. {{config}}), enabling Server-Side Template Injection. The template context also exposes Python built-ins (dir=dir, help=help, locals=locals), allowing escalation to remote code execution.

str(e) from a caught exception is interpolated into an HTML template string via %s formatting and passed to render_template_string(). Exception messages may contain user-controlled input from the search term, enabling Server-Side Template Injection. The template context also exposes Python built-ins (dir=dir, help=help, locals=locals), allowing escalation to remote code execution.

yaml.load(y) is called without specifying a safe Loader (PyYAML 3.12 defaults to the full Loader class that supports arbitrary Python object constructors). An attacker can upload a crafted YAML file containing !!python/object/apply: directives to execute arbitrary code on the server.

jwt.decode(token, verify=False) disables all JWT signature and claim verification. This function is used in the /get/<cust_id> route to authenticate requests (line 227), allowing an attacker to forge any JWT token and bypass authentication entirely.

request.url (user-controlled) is interpolated into an HTML template via %s string formatting before being rendered. Since the value is inserted into the template string before Jinja2 processing, auto-escaping does not apply, enabling Cross-Site Scripting.

str(e) is interpolated into an HTML template via %s string formatting before being rendered. Exception messages may contain user input from the search term, enabling Cross-Site Scripting since auto-escaping does not apply to values embedded before Jinja2 processing.

Three hardcoded secret keys are used: SECRET_KEY_HMAC='secret' (used for JWT signing), SECRET_KEY_HMAC_2='am0r3C0mpl3xK3y', and Flask secret_key='F12Zr47j\3yX R~X@H!jmM]Lwf/,?KT' (used for session signing). These are embedded in source code and can be used to forge JWT tokens and session cookies.
A default admin account is created with hardcoded credentials: username='admin', password='admin123'. These are embedded in source code and provide privileged access to the application.

MD5 (hashlib.md5) is used to hash passwords during registration. MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password hashing due to collision vulnerabilities and fast computation enabling brute-force attacks. No salt is used, making the hashes vulnerable to rainbow table attacks.

cwe: CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

extra.message: The /fetch/customer endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response without masking. Sensitive financial data should never be returned in full to clients.
The /get/<cust_id> endpoint returns the customer's credit card number (ccn) in the API response without masking. Sensitive financial data should never be returned in full to clients.

The /fetch/customer endpoint retrieves a customer record by ID (Customer.query.get(customer_id)) without verifying that the authenticated user is authorized to access that specific record. Any authenticated user can access any customer's data by changing the ID.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: Customer passwords are stored in plaintext in the database (passed directly as Customer(..., password, ...)). Unlike the User model which uses MD5 hashing, Customer passwords are stored without any hashing, exposing them if the database is compromised.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password

extra.message: The login endpoint compares the raw password from the request against the database value using filter_by(password=password). However, User passwords are stored as MD5 hashes (line 141), so this comparison will never match for legitimate users. An attacker who knows the MD5 hash (e.g., from a database leak) could use it directly as the password to authenticate.

Sensitive data is printed to logs: decoded JWT token contents (line 87), full request JSON including passwords (line 179), search terms (line 260), and uploaded file contents (line 305). This exposes sensitive information in application logs.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
